description: Grupo de estudiantes de la Universidad Católica Argentina, pertenecientes a la materia Labotario de Consultoría de Datos II. En este proyecto nos interesa aplicar técnicas de Ingeniería de datos y Machine Learning aprendidos en la materia.
summary:
Ghosts of the Solar System is a storytelling project about the machines NASA left behind on the Moon, Mars and in deep space. We compiled 45 pieces of equipment from NASA’s NSSDCA catalog and turned them into an interactive story where each machine tells its own tale, with a lifeline timeline showing how long it operated and why it stopped.

To go beyond the narrative, we added a survival analysis (Kaplan-Meier, log-rank tests and Cox models) on the 36 machines that operated autonomously, counting the 8 still active as censored data. It asks: how long does equipment last depending on its power source and destination? RTG-powered equipment lasted a median of ~14 years versus ~4 for solar, and deep-space missions outlasted lunar and Mars ones (~20 vs ~5 and ~4 years). RTG power cut the risk of ending operations by ~83%, even accounting for destination.

This matters because it turns “abandoned equipment” into evidence: what survives, what fails and why. That can inform the design of future long-duration missions and makes this history understandable for everyone.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
Ghosts of the Solar System tells the story of 45 machines NASA left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Each machine “speaks” for itself in the first person, and a lifeline timeline shows how long it operated and why it stopped. Behind the story sits a dataset built from NASA’s NSSDCA catalog and science.nasa.gov. It records each machine’s destination, power source, operating dates, planned versus actual duration, and cause of end. We added a survival analysis on the 36 machines that operated autonomously: 28 have ended and 8 are still active, which we treated as censored data. We used Kaplan-Meier curves to describe how long equipment lasts, log-rank tests to check that the differences are real, and Cox models to separate the effect of power source from the effect of destination.

What benefits does it have?
It turns a list of abandoned objects into evidence. RTG-powered equipment lasted a median of about 14 years versus about 4 for solar-powered equipment. Deep-space machines lasted about 20 years versus about 5 on the Moon and about 4 on Mars. Even for machines sent to the same destination, RTG power cut the risk of ending operations by about 83% (hazard ratio 0.17, 95% CI 0.06–0.46). The story makes this accessible to a general audience, and the analysis gives it a quantitative backbone.

What is the intended impact?
We want people to see abandoned equipment as a record of what survives, what fails and why, and not as space junk. That record can inform how future long-duration missions choose power sources and plan for harsh environments, and it makes space history understandable for people without a technical background.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Data: NASA’s NSSDCA catalog and science.nasa.gov, compiled into a CSV.
  • Analysis: Python in a Google Colab notebook, with pandas, lifelines (Kaplan-Meier, log-rank, Cox) and matplotlib.
  • Website: HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
  • Hardware: no special hardware, only standard computers and a browser.

How is it creative?
Two things combine that rarely appear together: voice and statistics. The machines tell their own stories, and the same data feeds a survival analysis, a method normally used in medicine, applied to spacecraft. A rover or probe is treated like a patient: it has a lifespan, a cause of death and a cohort to compare with. The visual identity (deep navy, NASA red and cyan) keeps the story and the charts consistent.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Which machines count. We excluded the 9 pieces that didn’t operate on their own (descent stages and crewed rovers), because their “duration” was a crew’s stay, not equipment lifetime.
  • Censoring. Active machines like the Voyagers, Curiosity and Perseverance were kept as censored cases, since ignoring them would underestimate lifespans.
  • Data limits. There are no autonomous battery-only machines, so the real comparison is RTG versus solar. The only passive equipment (the laser retroreflectors) can’t be compared on its own.
  • Confounding. Power source and destination are entangled, which is why we used a multivariable Cox model.
  • Failure versus decision. Some missions ended by human choice, not breakdown. We tested that in a sensitivity analysis.
  • Official list. We repeated the analysis using only the 24 autonomous machines on the challenge’s official resource list, and the RTG effect held (HR 0.15).
  • Small sample. With 28 events, the intervals are wide, so we read the results as direction and order of magnitude, and we say so openly.
dataRefs: Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars
